newsitem.title: USA: U.S. breast cancer experts fail to offer advice.
newsitem.headline: U.S. breast cancer experts fail to offer advice.

text.p: Amid bitter accusations of bias and conflict of interest, a panel of breast cancer experts on Thursday said women in their 40s must decide themselves whether to have mammograms.

The failure of an expert panel at a National Institutes of Health conference to recommend routine mammogram screening for breast cancer was described as "tantamount to a death sentence," by one radiologist.

A statement drafted by a 12-member panel of doctors, scientists and women's health advocates concluded: "... the available data do not warrant a single recommendation for mammography for all women in their 40s. Each woman should decide for herself whether to undergo mammography."

While the question of mammograms for women in their 40s is emotionally charged, there is general acknowledgment that mammograms can save the lives of women over 50, but are not generally appropriate for women under 40.
The panel added that if women in their 40s do choose to have mammograms, examinations costs should be paid by "third-party payors or covered by health maintenance organisations."
This did not go far enough for many of the hundreds of people who attended Thursday's public hearing on the issue.
"I do fear that this document is tantamount to a death sentence for thousands of women," Dr. Michael Livner, a New Mexico radiologist, said at the hearing.

Many in the audience questioned the panel's conclusion, saying the experts failed to take into account recent studies showing mammograms had significant benefits for women in their 40s. Some of these studies were presented to the panel on Tuesday and Wednesday.

Others protested that the committee's draft "consensus development conference statement" overstated the risks from the low-level radiation used to perform mammograms and understated the benefits of the procedure.

The experts wrote: "Not all women diagnosed with breast cancer by mammographic screening are helped by early detection ... Earlier detection may cause additional months or years of cancer-related anxiety, affecting personal relationships, insurance coverage and the workplace."

Mammography is far from an ideal technology. About 80 percent of the suspicious lesions spotted turn out to be harmless, but women still have to undergo invasive biopsies and huge stress to determine they are not cancerous.
